one_liner: The safe all rounder. Handles daily runs, treadmill sessions and the odd parkrun without fuss.
Thick, soft and forgiving underfoot. Great value if you want maximum comfort on easy runs.
Nike's softest everyday shoe. Bouncy foam that makes long, slow miles feel much easier.
Steady and supportive if your ankles roll inwards. Built to last a lot of miles.
A carbon plated trainer for faster sessions. Race day feel that survives everyday training.
Feather light race shoe for 5k up to marathon. Save it for the big days.
Nike's flagship marathon shoe. Springy air pods and a carbon plate for one big effort.
A road shoe feel with proper grip. Good for towpaths, parks and light trails.
Tough and grippy for muddy, rocky British trails. Underfoot protection without feeling clumsy.
Soft, protective and forgiving. The default choice for comfortable everyday miles.
Softer and cheaper than the Nimbus. A sensible first proper running shoe.
Bouncy and fun but still cushioned. Happy plodding along or picking up the pace.
The classic support shoe. Plush, stable and very hard to fall out with.
Gentle support at a fair price. A reliable starting point if you need stability.
Tall, light and lively. Expensive, but it can do almost every type of run.
Light carbon plated shoe for faster running. A cheaper way into race style shoes.
Very light racing shoe built for runners who lengthen their stride at speed.
A dependable everyday trail shoe. Good grip, decent cushioning and it lasts well.
Soft, roomy and easy going. Adidas' straightforward shoe for regular training runs.
Cushioned support with a generous fit. Quietly keeps your foot tracking straight.
Adidas' softest everyday cushion. Made for slow, comfortable miles rather than speed.
Light, springy and great value. A favourite for faster runs and shorter races.
Firm and purposeful with rods for push off. Best when you want to work.
Adidas' top marathon racer. Very light, very fast and fits on the narrow side.
Light and quick on the trails. Aimed at long off road races rather than beginners.
Waterproof and grippy for wet British winters. Keeps your feet dry on soggy paths.
Soft, light and easy to run in. Hoka's most popular everyday shoe for good reason.
About as much cushioning as you can buy. Great if your legs and joints ache.
Light and springy without being a race shoe. Good for picking up the pace.
Gentle support built in without feeling stiff. A light, friendly stability shoe.
Maximum support and cushioning together. Built for feet that roll inwards a lot.
Hoka's fastest carbon race shoe. Aggressive, expensive and only for race day.
The default trail shoe for muddy UK paths. Loads of grip and cushioning.
Half road shoe, half trail shoe. Ideal if your runs mix pavement and parks.
The safe, do everything trainer. If you are unsure what to buy, start here.
A big, wide, forgiving platform. Very stable underfoot and kind to sore joints.
Brooks at its softest. A pricey but very comfortable shoe for steady miles.
The classic support shoe. Sold in more widths than almost anything else out there.
The cheapest sensible Brooks. Firmer and lighter, and fine for a first pair.
Tall, bouncy and rolls you forward. A cheaper stand in for a race shoe.
Brooks' carbon plated racer. Very light, very fast, and saved for race day.
A tough, steady trail shoe with Vibram grip. Handles rough ground and wet rock.
A well balanced everyday shoe. Light enough to speed up, soft enough to plod.
Deep, soft cushioning that stays surprisingly light. One of the best long run shoes.
Quiet support that most people never notice. A good first stability shoe.
Loads of soft foam with support built in. Light for how much shoe it is.
A plated shoe you can actually train in every week. Fast but not fragile.
A proper carbon marathon racer that stays stable. Save it for your goal race.
Grippy, low to the ground and sure footed. Great on technical or muddy trails.
Cushioned trail shoe for very long days out. Heavy but protective and grippy.
Soft, roomy and light for its size. Comes in 2E and 4E widths.
A sturdy, no drama trainer that lasts. Widths up to 4E if you need room.
Solid, supportive and heavy. Best if you want obvious control and a roomy fit.
Light, bouncy and fun without a plate. A favourite for faster training runs.
A huge slab of soft foam. Made for slow, comfortable miles and recovery days.
New Balance's top marathon racer. Very light, very soft and built to go fast.
A plated, super cushioned trainer for marathon build ups. Soft with a forward roll.
Cushioned trail shoe with Vibram grip and rare wide fittings. Comfortable on rough ground.
Soft and easy going everyday shoe that suits steady runs and shorter distances.
Big, bouncy and fun underfoot, good for easy miles when your legs feel heavy.
Steady, supportive and forgiving, a safe first proper running shoe for most people.
Very light carbon plated racer built for going fast on race day.
Brilliant value all rounder that does easy runs and faster days without fuss.
One shoe that handles long runs, faster sessions and a half marathon happily.
Loads of soft foam underfoot, so long slow miles feel a lot kinder.
Firm rim around soft foam keeps wobbly ankles in line on longer runs.
Feather light race shoe for runners chasing a personal best over 10k or more.
Dependable everyday trainer that lasts well and rarely gives anyone trouble.
Classic support shoe for feet that roll inwards, tough and built to last.
Thick, soft and protective, a comfy pick for recovery runs and long days.
Tall stack with a plate, so long runs roll along quicker than expected.
Roomy toes and a completely flat platform, ease into it over a few weeks.
Wide toe room with a small heel lift, the friendliest way into Altra.
Cult trail shoe with masses of toe room and grippy Vibram rubber underneath.
Deep lugs that bite into mud, ideal for wet British winter trails.
Salomon's softest trail shoe, made for long days out when comfort matters most.
Gentle support with a wide front end, handy if your feet need space.
Flat, low and close to the ground with plenty of room for your toes.
Very soft and roomy up front, a rare mix of max cushion and toe space.
Light, simple and keenly priced, a solid choice for regular training runs.
Cushioned and steady, built for slow long runs rather than anything quick.
Made for proper mud, cross country and fell races where grip beats comfort.
The comfiest inov8, soft enough for all day hill days and long trail runs.
Last year's Clifton. Softer than it sounds and much cheaper than the 11.
The outgoing Ghost. Same safe everyday shoe, a slightly lower drop, far less money.
Last year's Triumph. A lot of soft foam for the money once it is discounted.
The outgoing Ride. A sensible, unfussy daily trainer at a much better price.
Last year's Nimbus. Still one of the softest shoes going, now heavily reduced.
The outgoing Cumulus. A quietly good everyday shoe that is now very cheap.
Last year's Pegasus. The same dependable all rounder for around half the price.
The outgoing 1080. Plush, wide fitting and a genuine bargain when reduced.
Last year's Guide. Probably the best value support shoe on the site right now.
The outgoing 860. Solid, steady support in wide fittings, now much cheaper.
Last year's ForeverRun. Support without feeling like a corrective shoe.
The outgoing Peregrine. Grippy and low to the ground, and a lot less money.
Last year's Cascadia. A tough, protective trail shoe for long days out.
The affordable Asics support shoe. Less foam than the Kayano, the same steadying idea.
Light, precise and built for racing on rough ground rather than plodding round it.
Waterproof, with a dial instead of laces. Built for wet British winters.
Asics at their cheapest. Fine for shorter runs and the gym, not for building big weeks.
The cheapest way into a proper running shoe. Light and simple, but it will not last long.
A plain, comfortable first running shoe at a sensible price.
A cheap way onto the trails. Heavy, but grippy enough for towpaths and light hills.
Budget trail shoe for easier off road runs rather than mountains.
Asics at a sensible price for everyday runs. It is snug across the toes, so try the wide fitting if that bothers you.
Nike's cheapest soft trainer. Forgiving underfoot for steady miles, and it comes in a 4E fitting.
Brooks at their cheapest, and the outsole wears unusually well. A sound first pair or a knockabout second shoe.
Low to the ground with a 4E fitting available. Better for shorter runs and the gym than for building big weeks.
The cheapest way into Asics support. Gentle guidance, hard wearing, and there is a 4E fitting.
The cheapest trail shoe here and a proper one. Firm and heavy, with enough grip for gravel and the odd rough bit.
Soft and light for a trail shoe, but the lugs are shallow. Made for dry paths and fire roads rather than mud.
Really a road shoe with a bit of tread. Light and cheap, but it wears out quickly and it is snug up front.
Waterproof, roomy up front and built to last. Fine on wet paths, but the tread is too shallow for real mud.
Tall, plush and stable underfoot for long easy miles. The plate is composite, not carbon.
Featherweight racer for 5k up to marathon, firm and narrow. No carbon, just a thin insert.
Adidas call the drop 6mm, the lab says 8mm. A road shoe with light grip for wet pavements.
Fast enough for tempo but happy on easy days too. Sources disagree on the drop, call it 6 to 7mm.
Cheap and versatile, but punishingly firm underfoot. Standard width only, with a low toebox.
The 48mm stack is illegal for official racing, and the drop measures 13mm, not the 7mm claimed.
A 5k to 10k racer with rods rather than a carbon plate. Narrow fit and very little heel support.
Under forty pounds, firm underfoot with a low 27mm heel. Best for lighter runners and walking.
Budget first shoe that lasts, though 318g is properly heavy and the toebox runs narrow.
Genuinely soft under a tall 45mm stack, and light with it. Not for anyone who needs toe room.
Road to trail at fifty pounds. Shallow lugs, so keep it to dry paths rather than proper mud.
Low and firm with a 3mm drop, not the 6mm claimed. Shallow lugs suit dry hard ground only.
Light trail racer for dry days. Runs narrow through the forefoot, and testers report toe rub.
Deeply rockered and soft for a trail shoe, with 4mm lugs. The thin upper needs looking after.
Waterproof and well armoured for wet winter miles. At 328g it plods rather than flies.
Effectively zero drop with a proper wide toebox. Firm underfoot, and not a first running shoe.
Zero drop racing with room for your toes. Thin heel padding and no cushioning to hide behind.
Vibram grip with 4mm lugs that cope with mud, plus a roomy toebox. Easy to get on with.
Soft and comfortable for long easy runs, but it measures 8mm drop, not the 4mm claimed.
Still zero drop despite the name, so ease into it. Cushioned, grippy and built for long days.
Piles on cushioning for all day trail use. Zero drop and 320g, so not a shoe to rush into.
Wide toebox, near zero drop and grip that lasts. Lugs are shallow, so think dry trails.
Firm and fast with almost no drop. Very little foam, so save it for shorter, quicker efforts.
High stacked and easygoing for daily miles, with a 10mm drop. The toebox is shallow on top.
Nimble on soft ground with 4mm lugs. The midsole is thin, so avoid long rocky routes.
Quick and firm on trail with a full length plate. Low on cushioning and it will not last long.
Sturdy and cheap for trail walks and easy miles. Asics publish no stack height for it.
Big, smooth cushioning for long slow miles. Be warned, the drop measures 11mm, not 6mm.
217g of speed with a genuinely roomy toebox. The upper is flimsy, so not a mileage shoe.
Plated and fast for long tempo work on a 45mm stack. Narrow through the toes, one width only.
Long trail days in comfort, with a rock plate and room for your toes. Lugs handle most ground.
Billed as max cushioned but the ride is firm. Deep lugs and plenty of stack for long trails.
A gentle first trail shoe that handles road to trail. Brooks publish no stack height.
The safe daily pick for any easy run. The foam is sold as springy but returns little energy.
Cushioned and easy for comfort miles, but it runs like a 9mm drop and the toebox is narrow.
Assertive support from full length GuideRails if your feet roll in. Dense, firm and 306g.
Maximum softness for long slow runs, at a hefty 318g. Measured drop is 8mm, not the 6mm claimed.
Very soft and good value, but a heel striker's shoe: the drop measures 12.5mm, not 6mm.
A tall daily shoe that suits heel strikers. Balanced rather than soft, and snug through the toes.
A Pebax plate for tempo days with enough foam left for long runs. Not a first shoe.
Heavy at 315g but built for long days on soft ground. An ultra shoe rather than a quick one.
Tall, carbon plated and 335g. Lugs are shallow, so gravel and road to trail, not technical ground.
Light and firm, especially at the forefoot. The thin outsole will not last as long as most.
Denser underfoot than it looks, with a snug toebox. Steady easy miles rather than plush comfort.
Soft PEBA foam over a carbon plate, but made for easy long miles rather than racing.
Huge cushioning and light guidance for road to trail. At 315g, not one for technical ground.
Light for a trail shoe, with deep 5mm lugs. Happy on soft ground and quick enough for efforts.
Firm, slim and quick over shorter trail races. Too little foam underfoot for ultra distances.
Low, firm and wide up front, with a rock plate for stony ground. Little help for heavier runners.
Roomy and hard wearing, but the grip disappoints for the money. Drop runs nearer 9mm than 6mm.
Deep 5.4mm lugs and a wide toebox for muddy days. Flexible, and taller than inov8 claims.
A firm minimalist racer on 6mm lugs. Very little underfoot, so build into it slowly.
Lugs are only 2.2mm, so keep it to dry paths and gravel. Narrow through the toes.
Barefoot feel, zero drop and 14mm underfoot. Only if your calves are already used to it.
Almost nothing between you and the ground at 8mm. Better for walking and gym than running.
The leather take on Merrell's barefoot shoe. Zero drop and 8mm of stack, so not for beginners.
Light and soft, aimed at comfort rather than bounce. The upper materials wear through quickly.
Very soft underfoot, which costs it some side to side steadiness. Widths from narrow up to 4E.
A cheap light trail shoe for paths and walks. Heavy at 331g, so nothing quick.
Very cheap and very light at 192g. Thin outsole and little protection, so gym and walking.
A forgiving budget everyday shoe with a high 10mm drop. Also sold in 2E and 4E widths.
Very soft and neutral, with no real side support. Drop is nearer 10mm than the claimed 8mm.
Carbon plated and 200g, made for 5k up to half marathon. Save it for the quick days.
A marathon racer whose drop measures almost 14mm, not 8mm. Thin outsole, so races only.
Quick and plated for tempo work. The drop measures nearer 9mm than the 4mm claimed.
Gravel and road to trail, with a hard wearing outsole. Lugs are too shallow for deep mud.
Waterproof, with 5mm Vibram lugs and a roomy toebox. A 350g tank, so nothing fast.
A marathon super shoe for race day only. The heel outsole wears fast if you land there.
Tall, soft and narrow, on a full length Air unit. Feels bottom heavy when you pick up pace.
Cheap, firm and stiff at the heel. Fine as a first shoe if your feet are on the narrow side.
Very firm with little impact protection. Cheap and stable, but not for heavier runners.
Deep, soft ZoomX for easy miles, but the toebox is sharply tapered. Skip it if your feet are wide.
Barely there at 128g, a 5k to 10k carbon racer. Forefoot strikers only, and it won't last long.
Marathon race day only. Nike claims 6mm drop but the lab measured 8.6mm, and the heel is narrow.
Big stack that rides firmer than it looks. A stable, hard wearing shoe for long, steady miles.
Very firm racer with a wide, squared off toebox. Too little give for heavier runners or beginners.
Firmer and heavier than a tempo shoe should be at 271g. The drop measures 4mm, not the claimed 6mm.
Heavy at 344g and very firm, but properly stable. Low volume inside, so not one for deep feet.
Light for a trail shoe at 225g. The 2mm lugs are for gravel and dry paths, never mud.
Only 37mm of firm foam despite the big name, with low energy return and a narrow toebox.
Hard wearing and firm for long days on gravel and hard pack. The 3mm lugs struggle in mud.
A light mountain racer at 229g, with a rock plate for technical ground. Built for ultra race days.
Steady trail shoe for easy off road miles. On won't publish a stack height, and the weight varies by source.
A 173g carbon racer for marathon day. The upper is thin and Puma's 40mm heel measured 37mm.
Comfort first for long, slow miles, and cheap at £129.99. The drop measures nearly 12mm, not 10mm.
Light and fairly firm daily trainer that runs narrow throughout. Good value if your feet are slim.
Road shoe that copes with gravel and hard pack. The 2.5mm lugs give up as soon as it gets muddy.
Cushioned daily miles, but Salomon's 8mm drop measured 11.7mm. Avoid it if you need a low drop.
Tall and cushioned for long trail days, with an outsole that barely wears. Lugs too shallow for mud.
4mm lugs and a TPU frame for rocky, technical ground. Gentle guidance without a proper support post.
Waterproof with 5mm lugs, so it really does handle mud. Heavy at 330g and low on cushioning.
A 346g tank for hard pack and hiking pace. Very supportive, but the drop measures 12.5mm, not 11mm.
Tall PWRRUN PB stack that lands firm rather than soft. The 8mm drop is exactly as claimed.
Ultra soft marathon racer at 197g and £279.99. Very little stability, so not for heavy or new runners.
Squishy top layer over a three quarter carbon plate. The toebox measures narrow at 70mm.
Stability in a trail shoe, with 3.5mm lugs that cope with softer ground. Heavy but comfortable.
Old school and firm at 207g. The thin outsole won't last, and it's too slight for heavier runners.
Plenty of soft foam for long, slow runs. The exposed midsole wore at 40 miles, so treat it gently.
Trail version of a familiar road trainer, with 3.5mm lugs. One width only, so fit matters.
Genuinely wide toebox and soft underfoot. Topo says 5mm drop, the lab measured 7mm, so mind your achilles.
Roomy and cushioned for long trail days, with Vibram grip. On the heavy side at 309g.
Soft foam on a wide, stable base with Megagrip and 3.7mm lugs. Too heavy at 315g for quick running.
Carbon racer with an unusual 2mm drop. Worth avoiding if your calves or achilles play up.
Simple, plateless tempo shoe at 212g and £119.99. The upper stretches, so it can feel loose in corners.
A 47mm slab of foam that stays springy instead of going mushy. The toebox is on the narrow side.
Built from recycled materials and priced like it. A steady everyday shoe, but nobody knows yet how far it lasts.
Adidasâ€™ marathon racer, 175g of carbon and foam. Narrow, delicate and strictly for race day.
Soft and tall for a trail shoe, with shallow tread. Made for hard paths and fire roads, not mud.
Carbon plated ultra racer with a roomy toebox. Fast on long mountain days, wasted on easy runs.
Light and roomy with proper lugs. Quick enough to race in, comfortable enough for long days out.
A carbon trail racer. Merrell say 6mm drop, the lab says 11mm, so treat it as a high drop shoe.
The Pegasus with a bouncier foam and a higher price. Easy miles rather than fast ones.
Steady and cushioned for long days on the trail. A little support built in without feeling corrective.
Built from Dyneema and priced accordingly. Tough, grippy and comfortable enough for all day efforts.
